items.name: .NET Framework 3.5
items.desc: The runtime a lot of older desktop software still asks for, including .NET 2.0 and 3.0 programs. Windows ships it disabled and fetches it on demand.
items.riskNote: The payload is not on the disk - Windows downloads it from Windows Update, so this needs a working internet connection and can take a few minutes. On a machine where update policy blocks the optional-content source it fails with error 0x800f0954 and changes nothing.

items.name: Windows Sandbox
items.desc: A throwaway Windows desktop in a window. Everything inside it disappears when you close it, which makes it the right place to run an installer you do not trust.
items.riskNote: Needs hardware virtualisation enabled in firmware. If it is off the feature installs and then refuses to start, and turning it on is a BIOS setting this toolkit cannot reach. Restart required.

items.name: Hyper-V
items.desc: Microsoft's virtual machine platform, with the management console.
items.riskNote: Turning Hyper-V on puts Windows itself on top of a hypervisor. VirtualBox and VMware still run but slower, and a handful of anti-cheat systems refuse to start with a hypervisor present. Needs hardware virtualisation enabled in firmware, and a restart.

items.name: Windows Subsystem for Linux
items.desc: Turns on the two features WSL needs. The distribution itself comes afterwards, from the Store or by running wsl --install -d Ubuntu.
items.riskNote: The Virtual Machine Platform half of this is the same hypervisor Hyper-V uses, with the same consequences for other virtual machine software and for anti-cheat. Restart required.

items.name: Telnet client
items.desc: The command-line telnet client, useful mostly for checking whether a port answers.

items.name: OpenSSH server
items.desc: Installs sshd so this machine can accept SSH connections. Installing it does not start it.
items.riskNote: Nothing listens until you start the sshd service and let it through the firewall, both of which are deliberately left to you. Once you do, this machine accepts remote sign-ins with your Windows credentials - only worth doing if you actually want that, and worth pairing with key-only authentication if you do.
